A1.justification: Both PDFs describe HybridFlow and provide readable main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices. Corresponding material can be matched despite revisions and pagination changes.

before.justification: Tables 1–3 report original benchmark and routing experiments; Appendix D also reports planner evaluation and fine-tuning results.

after.justification: V2 retains the original experiments and adds a GPQA evaluation with another edge/cloud model pair in Appendix D.2 and Table 7.

M1.justification: V1 explicitly does not optimize the dual variable during inference and uses a threshold calculated directly from resource consumption. V2 Section 3.3 instead specifies explicit dual updates and introduces online contextual-bandit utility calibration. This substantially changes the described routing procedure, although the appendices retain the older formulation.

E1.justification: Both versions use GPQA, MMLU-Pro, AIME24 and LiveBench-Reasoning, with the same MMLU-Pro/Math500 profiling data and s1k planning material. The new model-pair experiment retains GPQA and changes model configuration, without adding dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: Existing comparisons retain Direct Prompt, CoT, SoT, PASTA, HybridLLM and DoT, together with the same routing controls and planner comparators. Table 7 reuses CoT, HybridLLM and DoT with different underlying models. Newly cited related methods are not added experimental baselines.

E3.justification: Appendix D.2 adds a controlled GPQA evaluation using Qwen2.5-7B and DeepSeek-V3 instead of the main Llama3.2-3B/GPT-4.1 pair. It states that prompting, routing/scheduling, budgets and evaluation procedures are otherwise unchanged. Section 4.1 also now reports online router adaptation, although the appendix configuration remains inconsistent with that description.

E4.justification: The new model-pair swap tests whether the framework's trade-offs depend on its original model combination. Existing routing ablations, threshold sensitivity, offload-position analysis, planner fine-tuning comparison and case study are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions retain the same mean-and-standard-deviation reporting for main accuracy and latency results. No run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance procedures are added or revised. Table 7 uses point estimates, as existing supplementary tables already do.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3, 5 and 6 retain identical results. New Table 7 reports HybridFlow accuracy of 53%, API cost of $0.00116 and latency of 36.86 seconds under the swapped model pair; these are additional results under different conditions. Section 4.3 also corrects the stated utility-peak threshold from 0.5 to 0.6, matching unchanged Table 5.

T1.justification: The knapsack formulation and Lagrangian derivations are retained; the dual-update equation already appeared in v1. V2 adds the explicit dual-to-threshold mapping and calibration/reward formulas, plus a cloud-observer threat model and mathematical definitions of transmitted payload and token-based exposure in Appendix D.1. No new proof accompanies these additions.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion retain the central claims: dependency-aware parallel decomposition and adaptive resource-aware routing reduce latency and cloud usage while maintaining competitive accuracy. V2 foregrounds online adaptation, but adaptation to real-time resource budgets was already part of v1's contribution.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive qualifications: HybridFlow provides no formal privacy guarantee, and sensitive information can remain in offloaded subtasks or dependency answers. It also discusses utility miscalibration under shifts and interprets the model-pair experiment as limited transfer evidence, leaving broader model-family coverage unresolved.

D1.justification: V2 adds a code-availability link and explains cloud-request payloads. It removes v1's detailed decomposition Algorithm 2, including parsing and DAG-repair instructions, and omits the router's approximate 67M parameter count. Most existing training and hardware details remain; the new online-update configuration is incompletely specified.

R1.justification: Section 2 substantially revises the research positioning by acknowledging tree/graph reasoning through ToT, GoT and S-DAG, and budgeted cascades through FrugalGPT and mixture-of-thought representations. It expands discussion of SplitReason and foregrounds adaptation under changing conditions, replacing the earlier broader reasoning and collaboration discussion.

P1.justification: The introduction and related work are extensively rewritten, the optimization explanation and experimental setup are condensed, and the routing section is reorganized around offline estimation and online adaptation. V2 also adds named appendix subsections and updates the author and affiliation information.

P2.justification: V2 adds Table 7, removes the displayed Algorithm 2, and relocates retained tables and figures through reflow. Figure 4 changes its legend from 'Benefit-Cost Ratio' to 'Utility Score' while preserving the plotted results. The overall visual format remains similar, but some appendix equation references now display '??'.

improvement.justification: The model-pair experiment, explicit privacy limitations and closer prior-work comparisons improve the evidence and context. However, v2's new online router is not reconciled with the older policy retained in Appendices B–C or clearly linked to the unchanged main results. Removed decomposition pseudocode and unspecified online-update settings also weaken reproducibility. These material benefits and unresolved methodological inconsistencies prevent a reliable net quality judgment.
